lesson.title: Compartments of Complexity: Inside the Eukaryotic Cell
lesson.summary: Eukaryotic cells package their DNA inside a true nucleus and divide labor among a suite of membrane-bound organelles, an architecture that makes the large, complex cells of protists, fungi, plants, and animals possible.
lesson.body:
Cell theory again sets the stage: every organism is made of cells, and the cell is life's basic functional unit. Eukaryotic cells satisfy that rule with a very different strategy than the prokaryotic cells covered in the previous chapter. The name gives away the key feature: "eu" means true, and "karyon" refers to the nucleus, so a eukaryotic cell is defined by having a true, membrane-bound nucleus that houses its genetic material. Eukaryotic cells make up protists, fungi, plants, and animals, meaning every organism visible to the naked eye, including you, is built from this cell type.

The nucleus is only the most obvious of many internal compartments. Eukaryotic cells are subdivided by internal membranes into organelles, each specialized for a different job, much like rooms in a building are specialized for different tasks. Mitochondria break down sugars and generate most of the cell's usable energy in the form of ATP. The endoplasmic reticulum, rough where ribosomes are attached or smooth where they are not, builds proteins and lipids. The Golgi apparatus modifies, sorts, and packages those products for delivery. Lysosomes, found in animal cells, break down waste and worn-out cell parts using digestive enzymes. Plant cells add chloroplasts, which capture light energy and convert it into sugars, and a large central vacuole that manages water balance and storage.

This compartmentalization exists for real functional reasons, not just organization for its own sake. Keeping DNA inside a nuclear envelope separates transcription from translation, letting eukaryotic cells process and edit genetic messages before they are used to build proteins. Keeping digestive enzymes sealed inside a lysosome, and energy-releasing reactions sealed inside a mitochondrion, keeps those chemical processes from interfering with the rest of the cytoplasm. Compartments let very different chemical environments, acidic in one organelle, oxygen-rich in another, exist side by side within the same cell.

A widely accepted explanation for how two of these organelles arose is the endosymbiotic theory: mitochondria and chloroplasts likely began as free-living prokaryotic cells that were engulfed by a larger ancestral cell and, over evolutionary time, settled into a permanent, mutually beneficial partnership rather than being digested. Evidence for this includes the fact that both organelles carry their own small circular DNA and their own ribosomes, features expected of a formerly independent cell and not of an organelle built from scratch by its host.

All of this extra machinery takes up space, and eukaryotic cells are correspondingly larger than prokaryotic cells, typically ten to one hundred micrometers across rather than one to five. A human liver cell, for example, packs a nucleus, hundreds to thousands of mitochondria, an extensive endoplasmic reticulum, and a Golgi apparatus into a single cell built to process nutrients and toxins delivered by the bloodstream. That combination of larger size and greater internal organization is exactly what the next chapter examines, since size brings its own set of physical constraints that every eukaryotic cell has to work around.
